newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia closes independent Belgrade radio.
newsitem.headline: Serbia closes independent Belgrade radio.

text.p: Serbian authorities shut down Belgrade's only independent radio station B-92 on Tuesday amid a wave of opposition street protests against President Slobodan Milosevic, radio staff said.
The transmitter used by Radio B-92, which unlike state broadcasters had given wide coverage to the anti-government demonstrations, was switched off, editor-in-chief Veran Matic said.
The station received a letter from the federal ministry of transport and communication saying the radio was operating illegally, he said.

"This means our radio is practically shut down," Matic told Reuters. "This is obviously only the finish of what has been happening in the past 10 days, the stifling of B-92, an attempt to fully solve the "problem' of radio B-92."
The radio's signal was jammed for several days and went off the air as of 3 p.m. (1400 GMT) on Tuesday.

A student radio station, Radio Index, was also temporarily knocked off the air by the closure of the transmitter. The station, which has also covered the protests, still had legal permission to operate.
In contrast to state television and radio, Radio B-92 has provided live coverage of street demonstrations that have shaken Belgrade for more than two weeks.

The radio, one of a handful of independent radio stations in Serbia, complained that its signal was being jammed over the past several days and began sending news over the Internet in Serbo-Croat and English.
A global network of editors and publishers, the Vienna-based International Press Institute (IPI), condemned the closure.
The British government also deplored the decision to close the station, and called on the authorities in Belgrade to reconsider it.
"We urge the authorities to reverse their decision. It is important at this moment for independent democratic voices to be heard," the Foreign Office said.
The crackdown indicated Milosevic's government was taking an increasingly tough line to halt street demonstrations.
Accusations that ruling socialists committed massive poll fraud in local elections this month set off the protests, which analysts said had caused Milosevic political damage at home and abroad.
Milosevic last shut down Radio B-92 in 1991, when similar street demonstrations hit the capital. Police occupied the radio studio but B-92 resumed broadcasting within 24 hours.
Radio B-92 started operating on May 15, 1989 and its contract with state Radio Television Serbia expired in 1990. The station applied for a frequency but was never awarded a broadcasting license.
